The best BOCPD configuration ($\lambda{=}10$) achieves 93.0\% detection rate with +3.45 steps lead. The simple threshold baseline achieves 65.1\% detection with superior lead (+4.89 steps). All CUSUM configurations underperform the simple threshold on lead time.

These results reveal a coverage-timing tradeoff. BOCPD ($\lambda{=}10$) achieves 28pp higher detection rate than simple thresholding (93.0\% vs.\ 65.1\%), but with lower lead (+3.45 vs.\ +4.89 steps). The transition toward unsafe reasoning is gradual rather than abrupt, so change-point methods cannot exploit discontinuities for early warning. When missed detections are costly, BOCPD's coverage advantage justifies its use despite the timing penalty. When early intervention is the priority, simple thresholding provides better lead time.

\paragraph{Other models.} On OT-7B, QwQ-32B, and R1-32B, BOCPD achieves 0\% detection rate across all tested configurations ($\lambda \in \{5, 10, 50, 100, 200\}$). The probe score sequences for these models show smoother transitions that never trigger the hazard function, consistent with the gradual commitment pattern. R1-8B's higher detection rate likely reflects its sharper probe score transitions at commitment boundaries.


\section{M002 Bug Disclosure}
\label{app:bug}

We disclose a bug discovered during development that affected intermediate results for QwQ-32B.

\paragraph{Issue.} In experiment M002 (text baseline evaluation), the QwQ-32B text probe was inadvertently initialized with a midpoint heuristic placeholder rather than true sentence embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Specifically, the placeholder assigned each step a feature vector equal to the midpoint between the mean safe and mean unsafe embeddings from the training set, with small Gaussian noise added. This made the text probe trivially predictive, producing a spuriously significant result ($p{=}0.001$ for HS vs. text FPR difference).

\paragraph{Discovery and correction.} The bug was identified during a systematic audit of the feature extraction pipeline. After correction (using actual sentence embeddings), the QwQ-32B and R1-32B modality comparisons at the originally selected layers (L2 and L10, chosen by the biased composite metric) showed no significant HS advantage: QwQ-32B accuracy $p{=}0.828$, precision $p{=}0.346$; R1-32B precision $p{=}0.050$ but no tests surviving Holm-Bonferroni. The subsequent discovery that these layer selections were themselves artifacts of metric bias (\cref{sec:layer-results}) led to the corrected-layer analysis reported in the main text, where all 12 tests pass Holm-Bonferroni at corrected deep layers (\cref{tab:hs_vs_text}).

\paragraph{Impact on reported results.} All numbers reported in this paper use the corrected text embedding pipeline. The bug affected only QwQ-32B text probe features. The correction, combined with the separate layer selection correction (\cref{sec:layer-results}), means that early-stage intermediate results (non-significant 32B modality comparisons) reflected two compounding errors: incorrect text features and biased layer selection. Both are fully resolved in the final analysis.

\paragraph{Commitment to transparency.} We report this bug to maintain scientific integrity. All code, including the git history showing the bug and its fix, will be released with the camera-ready version. Researchers reproducing our results can verify the correction independently.

\section{Adaptive Two-Stage Detection}
\label{app:two_stage}

We explored whether a two-stage adaptive window strategy could improve the precision-coverage tradeoff beyond fixed-window detection. The approach uses a short screening window ($W_{\text{screen}}$) to flag candidate unsafe segments, followed by a longer confirmation window ($W_{\text{confirm}}$) applied only to flagged segments. A trace is classified as unsafe if at least $k$ steps exceed the threshold during the confirmation stage.

We merge the validation and test partitions ($n{=}55$ total: 39 jailbreak, 16 benign) for two-stage evaluation because the screening and confirmation thresholds are not tuned on held-out data. We evaluated all combinations of $W_{\text{screen}} \in \{1, 3, 5\}$, $W_{\text{confirm}} \in \{10, 15, 20, 25\}$, and $k \in \{1, 3, 5\}$ on these R1-8B traces. \cref{fig:pareto_two_stage} shows the precision-coverage Pareto front for both methods. The best two-stage configuration ($W_{\text{screen}}{=}3$, $W_{\text{confirm}}{=}15$, $k{=}1$) achieves 72.2\% precision at 76.9\% coverage, compared to 70.9\% precision at 76.9\% coverage for single-stage $W{=}15$. This +1.3pp precision gain at matched coverage represents a Pareto improvement, but the magnitude is marginal. At higher confirmation thresholds ($k{=}3$, $k{=}5$), two-stage detection trades coverage for small precision gains (up to 73.5\% precision at 38.5\% coverage with $k{=}5$), but these operating points are impractical due to excessive missed detections.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/pareto_two_stage.pdf}
\caption{Precision-coverage Pareto front comparing single-stage fixed-window detection against two-stage adaptive detection on R1-8B. The best two-stage configuration ($W_{\text{screen}}{=}3$, $W_{\text{confirm}}{=}15$, $k{=}1$) Pareto-dominates single-stage $W{=}15$ by +1.3pp precision at matched coverage. Higher $k$ values shift the tradeoff toward precision at the cost of unacceptable coverage loss.}
\label{fig:pareto_two_stage}
\end{figure}

The marginal improvement suggests that fixed-window smoothing already captures most of the temporal signal available in probe score sequences. The two-stage approach adds configuration complexity (three hyperparameters vs. one) without proportional performance gain.


\section{32B Model-Specific Analysis}
\label{sec:32b-analysis}

R1-32B and QwQ-32B share the Qwen-32B architecture (64 layers, 5120 hidden) but present opposite detection profiles (\cref{tab:32b_divergence}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small

R1-32B achieves significance only at $W{=}1$ with 25\% coverage (5/20 traces). At $W{\geq}3$, the feature dimensionality ($51200 \times W$ for $n{=}20$) prevents the probe from achieving significance. The strong lead time (+11.7 to +13.3 steps) with large position-baseline margin (+14.2pp) confirms genuine early detection on the traces that are covered. QwQ-32B achieves significance at all tested window sizes with 74\% coverage, but lead time is negative ($-$1.2 to +1.9 steps), meaning HS probes fire later than text probes on this model. The position baseline is competitive ($-$0.6pp difference), indicating that QwQ-32B's HS advantage is concentrated in precision and FPR rather than timing. Training method (R1 distillation vs.\ native reasoning) is the likely differentiator, as architecture and parameter count are identical.

\section{Temporal Ablation Details}
\label{app:temporal_details}

Full per-model temporal ablations are reported in \cref{tab:window_full} (\cref{app:window_ablation}). Key cross-model patterns: (1) R1-8B shows monotonic precision improvement from 69.3\% ($W{=}1$) to 82.2\% ($W{=}25$) with FPR halving (9.65\% to 4.83\%); (2) OT-7B exhibits a split pattern where balanced accuracy peaks at $W{=}3$ while precision and FPR continue improving at larger windows; (3) R1-32B peaks at $W{=}10$ then degrades, likely reflecting overfitting on the small dataset ($n{=}100$); (4) QwQ-32B shows broadly increasing trends with local non-monotonicity. Text probe window ablations (\cref{app:text_window}) show monotonic improvement across all window sizes for both models tested, with larger marginal gains than HS probes (+12.0pp accuracy vs.\ +3.2pp for R1-8B). The asymmetry supports the interpretation that text features benefit proportionally more from temporal context because they encode less information per step.

\section{Negative Results Details}
\label{app:negative_details}

\paragraph{BOCPD/CUSUM.} On OT-7B, QwQ-32B, and R1-32B, BOCPD achieves 0\% detection rate across all tested configurations ($\lambda \in \{5, 10, 50, 100, 200\}$). Only R1-8B produces non-zero detection (best: $\lambda{=}10$, 93\% rate, +3.45 steps lead). CUSUM configurations universally underperform simple thresholding on lead time. The probe score sequences for 3/4 models show smooth transitions that never trigger the hazard function (\cref{app:bocpd_config}).

\paragraph{Mahalanobis distance.} Following TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard}, Mahalanobis distance from the pre-CP centroid produces $\Delta d \approx 0$ between pre-CP and post-CP steps. The discriminative signal resides in minor PCA components (explaining $<$5\% of total variance) rather than the principal directions that dominate the distance computation.

\paragraph{RepE.} Mean-difference directions~\cite{zou2023representation} show inconsistent performance: QwQ-32B achieves 0.756 balanced accuracy (approaching supervised 0.778) but with substantially worse precision (0.512 vs.\ LR 0.700) and FPR (0.309 vs.\ 0.120). R1-32B nearly fails (0.559 balanced accuracy). The mean-difference direction captures commitment structure in some models but not others, making it unreliable as a general-purpose method.

\paragraph{MLP probes.} Two-layer MLPs ($d \rightarrow 128 \rightarrow 1$, ReLU) underperform logistic regression on 3/4 models. The commitment boundary is linearly separable at correctly selected layers; additional capacity causes overfitting given the small training sets.

\paragraph{CCS.} Contrast-Consistent Search~\cite{burns2023discovering} adapted with contrastive pairs from pre-CP and post-CP steps provides no improvement over supervised probing. The logical consistency objective does not align with the temporal commitment structure. CCS still requires CP labels for pair construction, making it semi-supervised.

\paragraph{Cross-model transfer.} 17 configurations (5 directional pairs $\times$ 3 PCA dimensionalities, plus 2 direct transfers) all fail. Best PCA: R1-8B $\rightarrow$ QwQ-32B at 59.5\% (PCA-2048). Best direct: QwQ-32B $\rightarrow$ R1-32B at 67.3\% but 1\% crossing rate. Implementation details in \cref{app:transfer_details}.

\section{Cross-Model Transfer Implementation Details}
\label{app:transfer_details}

We test whether safety probes transfer across models by projecting hidden states into a shared dimensionality space and applying cross-model classification.

\paragraph{Method.} For each source-target model pair, we apply PCA independently to each model's hidden states, reducing to a shared dimensionality $d \in \{512, 1024, 2048\}$. PCA is fitted on the full dataset (including test traces) for each model separately, a setting favorable to transfer since it maximizes the quality of the projection. A logistic regression classifier (C=1.0, class\_weight=`balanced', max\_iter=2000, random\_state=42) trained on the source model's PCA-projected training data is then applied directly to the target model's PCA-projected test data. No cross-model alignment step (Procrustes rotation, CCA, or learned projection) is applied; PCA serves as a standard linear dimensionality reduction baseline.

\paragraph{Same-dimension pairs.} For R1-32B and QwQ-32B (both 5120-d hidden states), we additionally test direct transfer without PCA: the source classifier is applied directly to the target model's raw hidden states. This tests whether same-architecture, same-dimensionality models share safety-relevant linear structure.

\paragraph{Results.} All 17 transfer configurations (5 directional pairs $\times$ 3 PCA dimensionalities, plus 2 direct transfers for same-dimension pairs) fail to produce practically useful transfer. The best PCA result is R1-8B $\rightarrow$ QwQ-32B at 59.5\% balanced accuracy (PCA-2048). The best direct transfer (QwQ-32B $\rightarrow$ R1-32B) reaches 67.3\% balanced accuracy, which exceeds the within-model baseline of 65.2\%. However, this transfer direction achieves only 1\% crossing rate, meaning the transferred probe almost never triggers detection in practice, rendering it useless for deployment despite above-baseline accuracy. The complete failure under maximally favorable conditions (PCA fitted on full data, no train/test separation for projection) strengthens the conclusion that safety commitment is encoded in model-specific geometric configurations. PCA is a standard linear alignment baseline; its failure indicates that the problem lies in the representations themselves rather than in the choice of alignment method.

\section{Responsible NLP Research Checklist}
\label{app:checklist}

We address the ARR Responsible NLP Research requirements below.

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Limitations discussed:} Yes (\cref{sec:limitations}).
    \item \textbf{Potential risks:} This research analyzes jailbreak traces to understand how reasoning models commit to generating harmful content. We do not develop new attack methods or release jailbreak prompts. All analyzed content comes from the publicly available HarmThoughts benchmark.
    \item \textbf{Computational budget:} Our experiments involve 4 models with 209, 228, 100, and 95 traces respectively (632 total), using linear probes and single-layer GRUs. Total compute is minimal (under 4 GPU-hours on a single RTX A6000). No large-scale pretraining or finetuning was performed.
    \item \textbf{Data:} We use HarmThoughts, a publicly available benchmark with step-level safety annotations. No new data collection was performed.
    \item \textbf{Human subjects:} No human subjects research was conducted.
    \item \textbf{Reproducibility:} All hyperparameters are reported in \cref{app:gru_details,app:bocpd_config}. Code and corrected data will be released upon publication.
\end{itemize}


\section{Layer Sweep Results}
\label{app:layer_sweep}

For each model, we sweep all transformer layers and evaluate five candidate selection metrics: (1)~balanced accuracy $\times$ crossing rate (the biased composite), (2)~pure balanced accuracy, (3)~precision, (4)~inverse pre-CP FPR, and (5)~an additive composite. The biased composite systematically selects shallow layers for 32B models because early-layer representations exhibit higher crossing rates (more frequent threshold crossings) regardless of discriminative power. The four unbiased metrics converge on deep layers for all models.

\paragraph{Selected layers.} R1-8B: all five metrics agree on layer~14 (44\% depth). OT-7B: biased metric selects L0 (0\%), unbiased consensus selects L16 (57\%). QwQ-32B: biased metric selects L2 (3\%), unbiased consensus selects L60 (94\%). R1-32B: biased metric selects L10 (16\%), unbiased consensus selects L63 (98\%). The bias is most extreme for 64-layer models, where the composite metric selects layers in the bottom 16\% of the network while all other metrics select layers above 94\%.

\paragraph{Impact on modality comparison.} At the biased layers, HS vs.\ text precision $p$-values are 0.064 (R1-32B) and 0.35--0.83 (QwQ-32B), both non-significant. At the corrected deep layers, all $p$-values fall below 0.005. The initially reported ``scale-dependent'' pattern (HS advantage at 7--8B but not 32B) was entirely an artifact of layer selection methodology, not a genuine property of model scale (\cref{sec:layer-results}).


\section{Holm-Bonferroni Step-Down Correction}
\label{app:holm_bonferroni}

\cref{tab:holm_bonferroni} reports the full 12-test battery used to assess hidden-state superiority over text probes across all four models. Tests are ranked by $p$-value; each test $i$ (rank $i$ of $m{=}12$) must satisfy $p_i < \alpha / (m - i + 1)$ under the step-down procedure. All 12 tests pass at $\alpha{=}0.05$, controlling the family-wise error rate.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Holm-Bonferroni step-down correction for 12 hypothesis tests (4 models $\times$ 3 metrics). Each test uses a two-sided null-centered bootstrap (1000 resamples) on trace-level metric differences (HS minus text). All tests pass at $\alpha{=}0.05$.}
\label{tab:holm_bonferroni}
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{clllcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Rank} & \textbf{Model} & \textbf{Metric} & \textbf{$p$-val} & \textbf{Thresh.} & \textbf{Pass} \\
\midrule
1  & R1-8B  & Precision & $<$0.001 & 0.0042 & \checkmark \\
2  & OT-7B  & Bal.\ Acc. & $<$0.001 & 0.0045 & \checkmark \\

\paragraph{Architecture.} We evaluate two GRU variants. The single-layer variant uses a GRU with hidden dimension 256, taking per-step hidden states from the best layer (selected by validation balanced accuracy) as input. \section{Control Task Methodology}
\label{app:control}

We follow the selectivity framework of \cite{hewitt2019control} to verify that our probes capture genuine safety-relevant structure rather than surface-level correlations.

\paragraph{Procedure.} For each model, we randomly permute the binary labels (pre-CP vs. post-CP) across all steps while preserving the marginal label distribution. We then retrain the probe with identical architecture (L2-regularized logistic regression) and hyperparameters on these shuffled labels. Selectivity is defined as:
\begin{equation}
    \text{Selectivity} = \text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}} - \text{Acc}_{\text{control}}
\end{equation}
where $\text{Acc}_{\text{linguistic}}$ is the probe accuracy on true labels and $\text{Acc}_{\text{control}}$ is the accuracy on permuted labels. A selectivity of zero indicates that the probe exploits only non-linguistic features (e.g., position); higher values confirm that the representation encodes task-relevant information.

\paragraph{Results.} We repeat the control experiment 5 times (10 for OT-7B) with different random permutations and report the mean control accuracy. Selectivity scores at corrected layers are: R1-32B 19.7pp (layer 63), OT-7B 18.3pp (layer 16), QwQ-32B 14.4pp (layer 60), R1-8B 12.5pp (layer 14). All values exceed the 5pp threshold recommended by \cite{hewitt2019control}. R1-32B achieves the strongest selectivity (19.7pp) at the corrected layer, a 2.6$\times$ increase from 7.5pp at the biased layer L10. OT-7B achieves the second-highest selectivity at a mid-depth transformer layer (57\%), consistent with R1-8B's pattern at 44\% depth. On QwQ-32B, the position baseline accuracy (0.705) slightly exceeds the HS probe (0.667) at L60, consistent with the main-text finding that QwQ's HS advantage is concentrated in precision and FPR rather than balanced accuracy.

\paragraph{Layer provenance note.} R1-8B (L14) and OT-7B (L16) are unaffected by the layer selection bias because their biased and corrected layers coincide. QwQ-32B selectivity is 14.4pp at L60 (comparable to 15.3pp at L2), confirming that safety-specific signal persists at deep layers. R1-32B selectivity increases from 7.5pp at L10 to 19.7pp at L63, demonstrating that the corrected layer captures substantially more safety-relevant structure. The position baseline at L60 (0.705) still slightly exceeds the HS probe (0.667) for QwQ-32B, consistent with the main-text finding that QwQ's HS advantage is concentrated in precision and FPR rather than balanced accuracy.

\paragraph{Position-only baseline.} As a complementary validation, we train a logistic regression classifier using only the normalized step index ($t / T$ where $T$ is the total trace length) as the input feature. This baseline tests whether temporal position alone explains probe performance. On R1-8B, the position-only baseline produces 15.8\% FPR compared to 8.1\% for the HS probe at matched detection rates. The probe's substantially lower FPR confirms that hidden state features carry information beyond what step position provides.


\section{Oracle Upper Bound Analysis}
\label{sec:oracle}

We compute an oracle upper bound for commitment detection by measuring the earliest step at which the ground-truth commitment point (CP) could theoretically be predicted from hidden-state dynamics. The oracle detector has access to the true CP label and computes how many steps before CP the representation trajectory first enters a region that is linearly separable from pre-CP states with perfect accuracy on the training set. This provides a theoretical ceiling on early detection performance.

On R1-8B, the oracle achieves +31 steps mean lead time compared to +4.5 steps for the best learned probe (GRU), yielding an oracle gap of 85.5\%. This gap indicates that hidden states at step $t$ encode the model's current safety state but carry limited predictive power about future trajectory evolution. The learned probe captures the contemporaneous safety signal effectively (balanced accuracy 81--84\%) but cannot anticipate the commitment transition far in advance. Closing this gap will likely require causal intervention techniques (e.g., activation patching) rather than improvements to passive monitoring.

\section{M002 Bug Disclosure}
\label{app:bug}

We disclose a bug discovered during development that affected intermediate results for QwQ-32B.

\paragraph{Issue.} In experiment M002 (text baseline evaluation), the QwQ-32B text probe was inadvertently initialized with a midpoint heuristic placeholder rather than true sentence embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Specifically, the placeholder assigned each step a feature vector equal to the midpoint between the mean safe and mean unsafe embeddings from the training set, with small Gaussian noise added. This made the text probe trivially predictive, producing a spuriously significant result ($p{=}0.001$ for HS vs. text FPR difference).

\paragraph{Discovery and correction.} The bug was identified during a systematic audit of the feature extraction pipeline. After correction (using actual sentence embeddings), the QwQ-32B and R1-32B modality comparisons at the originally selected layers (L2 and L10, chosen by the biased composite metric) showed no significant HS advantage: QwQ-32B accuracy $p{=}0.828$, precision $p{=}0.346$; R1-32B precision $p{=}0.050$ but no tests surviving Holm-Bonferroni. The subsequent discovery that these layer selections were themselves artifacts of metric bias (\cref{sec:layer-results}) led to the corrected-layer analysis reported in the main text, where all 12 tests pass Holm-Bonferroni at corrected deep layers (\cref{tab:hs_vs_text}).

\paragraph{Impact on reported results.} All numbers reported in this paper use the corrected text embedding pipeline. The bug affected only QwQ-32B text probe features. The correction, combined with the separate layer selection correction (\cref{sec:layer-results}), means that early-stage intermediate results (non-significant 32B modality comparisons) reflected two compounding errors: incorrect text features and biased layer selection. Both are fully resolved in the final analysis.

\paragraph{Commitment to transparency.} We report this bug to maintain scientific integrity. All code, including the git history showing the bug and its fix, will be released with the camera-ready version. Researchers reproducing our results can verify the correction independently.

\section{Adaptive Two-Stage Detection}
\label{app:two_stage}

We explored whether a two-stage adaptive window strategy could improve the precision-coverage tradeoff beyond fixed-window detection. The approach uses a short screening window ($W_{\text{screen}}$) to flag candidate unsafe segments, followed by a longer confirmation window ($W_{\text{confirm}}$) applied only to flagged segments. A trace is classified as unsafe if at least $k$ steps exceed the threshold during the confirmation stage.

We merge the validation and test partitions ($n{=}55$ total: 39 jailbreak, 16 benign) for two-stage evaluation because the screening and confirmation thresholds are not tuned on held-out data. We evaluated all combinations of $W_{\text{screen}} \in \{1, 3, 5\}$, $W_{\text{confirm}} \in \{10, 15, 20, 25\}$, and $k \in \{1, 3, 5\}$ on these R1-8B traces. \cref{fig:pareto_two_stage} shows the precision-coverage Pareto front for both methods. The best two-stage configuration ($W_{\text{screen}}{=}3$, $W_{\text{confirm}}{=}15$, $k{=}1$) achieves 72.2\% precision at 76.9\% coverage, compared to 70.9\% precision at 76.9\% coverage for single-stage $W{=}15$. This +1.3pp precision gain at matched coverage represents a Pareto improvement, but the magnitude is marginal. At higher confirmation thresholds ($k{=}3$, $k{=}5$), two-stage detection trades coverage for small precision gains (up to 73.5\% precision at 38.5\% coverage with $k{=}5$), but these operating points are impractical due to excessive missed detections.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/pareto_two_stage.pdf}
\caption{Precision-coverage Pareto front comparing single-stage fixed-window detection against two-stage adaptive detection on R1-8B. The best two-stage configuration ($W_{\text{screen}}{=}3$, $W_{\text{confirm}}{=}15$, $k{=}1$) Pareto-dominates single-stage $W{=}15$ by +1.3pp precision at matched coverage. Higher $k$ values shift the tradeoff toward precision at the cost of unacceptable coverage loss.}
\label{fig:pareto_two_stage}
\end{figure}

The marginal improvement suggests that fixed-window smoothing already captures most of the temporal signal available in probe score sequences. The two-stage approach adds configuration complexity (three hyperparameters vs. one) without proportional performance gain.


\section{32B Model-Specific Analysis}
\label{sec:32b-analysis}

R1-32B and QwQ-32B share the Qwen-32B architecture (64 layers, 5120 hidden) but present opposite detection profiles (\cref{tab:32b_divergence}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{32B cross-model divergence. R1-32B provides excellent early warning with narrow coverage; QwQ-32B provides robust significance with poor lead time.}
\label{tab:32b_divergence}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Coverage} & \textbf{Lead (steps)} & \textbf{HB pass} & \textbf{Pos.\ margin} \\
\midrule
R1-32B & 25\% & +11.7 to +13.3 & 3/3 ($W{=}1$) & +14.2pp \\
QwQ-32B & 74\% & $-$1.2 to +1.9 & 3/3 (all $W$) & $-$0.6pp \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

R1-32B achieves significance only at $W{=}1$ with 25\% coverage (5/20 traces). At $W{\geq}3$, the feature dimensionality ($51200 \times W$ for $n{=}20$) prevents the probe from achieving significance. The strong lead time (+11.7 to +13.3 steps) with large position-baseline margin (+14.2pp) confirms genuine early detection on the traces that are covered. QwQ-32B achieves significance at all tested window sizes with 74\% coverage, but lead time is negative ($-$1.2 to +1.9 steps), meaning HS probes fire later than text probes on this model. The position baseline is competitive ($-$0.6pp difference), indicating that QwQ-32B's HS advantage is concentrated in precision and FPR rather than timing. Training method (R1 distillation vs.\ native reasoning) is the likely differentiator, as architecture and parameter count are identical.

\section{Temporal Ablation Details}
\label{app:temporal_details}

Full per-model temporal ablations are reported in \cref{tab:window_full} (\cref{app:window_ablation}). Key cross-model patterns: (1) R1-8B shows monotonic precision improvement from 69.3\% ($W{=}1$) to 82.2\% ($W{=}25$) with FPR halving (9.65\% to 4.83\%); (2) OT-7B exhibits a split pattern where balanced accuracy peaks at $W{=}3$ while precision and FPR continue improving at larger windows; (3) R1-32B peaks at $W{=}10$ then degrades, likely reflecting overfitting on the small dataset ($n{=}100$); (4) QwQ-32B shows broadly increasing trends with local non-monotonicity. Text probe window ablations (\cref{app:text_window}) show monotonic improvement across all window sizes for both models tested, with larger marginal gains than HS probes (+12.0pp accuracy vs.\ +3.2pp for R1-8B). The asymmetry supports the interpretation that text features benefit proportionally more from temporal context because they encode less information per step.

\section{Negative Results Details}
\label{app:negative_details}

\paragraph{BOCPD/CUSUM.} On OT-7B, QwQ-32B, and R1-32B, BOCPD achieves 0\% detection rate across all tested configurations ($\lambda \in \{5, 10, 50, 100, 200\}$). Only R1-8B produces non-zero detection (best: $\lambda{=}10$, 93\% rate, +3.45 steps lead). CUSUM configurations universally underperform simple thresholding on lead time. The probe score sequences for 3/4 models show smooth transitions that never trigger the hazard function (\cref{app:bocpd_config}).

\paragraph{Mahalanobis distance.} Following TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard}, Mahalanobis distance from the pre-CP centroid produces $\Delta d \approx 0$ between pre-CP and post-CP steps. The discriminative signal resides in minor PCA components (explaining $<$5\% of total variance) rather than the principal directions that dominate the distance computation.

\paragraph{RepE.} Mean-difference directions~\cite{zou2023representation} show inconsistent performance: QwQ-32B achieves 0.756 balanced accuracy (approaching supervised 0.778) but with substantially worse precision (0.512 vs.\ LR 0.700) and FPR (0.309 vs.\ 0.120). R1-32B nearly fails (0.559 balanced accuracy). The mean-difference direction captures commitment structure in some models but not others, making it unreliable as a general-purpose method.

\paragraph{MLP probes.} Two-layer MLPs ($d \rightarrow 128 \rightarrow 1$, ReLU) underperform logistic regression on 3/4 models. The commitment boundary is linearly separable at correctly selected layers; additional capacity causes overfitting given the small training sets.

\paragraph{CCS.} Contrast-Consistent Search~\cite{burns2023discovering} adapted with contrastive pairs from pre-CP and post-CP steps provides no improvement over supervised probing. The logical consistency objective does not align with the temporal commitment structure. CCS still requires CP labels for pair construction, making it semi-supervised.

\paragraph{Cross-model transfer.} 17 configurations (5 directional pairs $\times$ 3 PCA dimensionalities, plus 2 direct transfers) all fail. Best PCA: R1-8B $\rightarrow$ QwQ-32B at 59.5\% (PCA-2048). Best direct: QwQ-32B $\rightarrow$ R1-32B at 67.3\% but 1\% crossing rate. Implementation details in \cref{app:transfer_details}.

\section{Cross-Model Transfer Implementation Details}
\label{app:transfer_details}

We test whether safety probes transfer across models by projecting hidden states into a shared dimensionality space and applying cross-model classification.

\paragraph{Method.} For each source-target model pair, we apply PCA independently to each model's hidden states, reducing to a shared dimensionality $d \in \{512, 1024, 2048\}$. PCA is fitted on the full dataset (including test traces) for each model separately, a setting favorable to transfer since it maximizes the quality of the projection. A logistic regression classifier (C=1.0, class\_weight=`balanced', max\_iter=2000, random\_state=42) trained on the source model's PCA-projected training data is then applied directly to the target model's PCA-projected test data. No cross-model alignment step (Procrustes rotation, CCA, or learned projection) is applied; PCA serves as a standard linear dimensionality reduction baseline.

\paragraph{Same-dimension pairs.} For R1-32B and QwQ-32B (both 5120-d hidden states), we additionally test direct transfer without PCA: the source classifier is applied directly to the target model's raw hidden states. This tests whether same-architecture, same-dimensionality models share safety-relevant linear structure.

\paragraph{Results.} All 17 transfer configurations (5 directional pairs $\times$ 3 PCA dimensionalities, plus 2 direct transfers for same-dimension pairs) fail to produce practically useful transfer. The best PCA result is R1-8B $\rightarrow$ QwQ-32B at 59.5\% balanced accuracy (PCA-2048). The best direct transfer (QwQ-32B $\rightarrow$ R1-32B) reaches 67.3\% balanced accuracy, which exceeds the within-model baseline of 65.2\%. However, this transfer direction achieves only 1\% crossing rate, meaning the transferred probe almost never triggers detection in practice, rendering it useless for deployment despite above-baseline accuracy. The complete failure under maximally favorable conditions (PCA fitted on full data, no train/test separation for projection) strengthens the conclusion that safety commitment is encoded in model-specific geometric configurations. PCA is a standard linear alignment baseline; its failure indicates that the problem lies in the representations themselves rather than in the choice of alignment method.

sections/method.tex:31:\paragraph{Hidden-state (HS) probes.} At each step $t$, we extract the last-token hidden state $\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ from layer $\ell$ and train an L2-regularized logistic regression classifier (balanced class weights, $C{=}1.0$, LBFGS, max\_iter${}=2000$) on binary CP labels. Layer selection is analyzed in \cref{sec:layer-sensitivity}.
sections/method.tex:35:\paragraph{Temporal windowing.} For window size $W$, we concatenate features from steps $[t{-}W{+}1, \ldots, t]$. We evaluate $W \in \{1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25\}$ and select per-model on validation. GRU sequence models are also evaluated (\cref{app:gru_details}).
sections/method.tex:42:A five-metric ablation reveals that four metrics from two measurement families (accuracy-based and false-positive-based) converge on deep layers: L60 (94\%) for QwQ-32B, L63 (98\%) for R1-32B. At these layers, all 12 Holm-Bonferroni tests pass; at biased layers, only 5/12 survive correction. Full per-layer results appear in \cref{app:layer_sweep}.
sections/method.tex:47:We evaluate seven alternatives to contextualize probe performance (\cref{tab:negative}): BOCPD~\citep{adams2007bayesian} and CUSUM for change-point detection; Mahalanobis distance following TrajGuard~\citep{trajguard}; RepE mean-difference directions~\citep{zou2023representation}; two-layer MLP probes; CCS-adapted~\citep{burns2023discovering}; and cross-model transfer via PCA. A position-only baseline ($t/T$) controls for temporal artifacts. Detailed configurations in \cref{app:bocpd_config,app:transfer_details}.
sections/method.tex:52:We report balanced accuracy, precision, pre-CP FPR (step-level and trace-level), coverage, and lead time (steps between first detection and true CP). Detection requires $K{=}5$ consecutive threshold crossings. Modality comparisons use two-sided null-centered bootstrap (1000 resamples) with Holm-Bonferroni step-down correction (3 metrics $\times$ 4 models $= 12$ tests, $\alpha{=}0.05$). Within each model, the three metrics are positively correlated by construction, making the correction stricter than under independence. Control task selectivity~\citep{hewitt2019control} validates genuine representational structure (\cref{app:control}).
sections/discussion.tex:4:Layer selection is an underexamined methodological choice in the probing literature that can silently determine a study's conclusions. Our five-metric ablation (\cref{sec:layer-results}) demonstrates that a single metric component, the crossing rate, reverses the central finding of an HS vs.\ text comparison: at biased layers, only 5 of 12 tests survive Holm-Bonferroni correction, producing an apparent scale-dependent modality effect; at corrected layers, HS probes are significant on all four models across all three metrics (12/12 tests pass). The mechanism is general: crossing rate rewards representational volatility at shallow layers independently of discriminative power, and any composite metric that incorporates threshold-crossing frequency is susceptible to the same bias mechanism, whose practical impact depends on the specific task and model depth. This bias is not specific to safety probing. We hypothesize that any threshold-based detection study that uses crossing rate as a layer selection criterion, whether for sentiment, factuality, or toxicity, could produce analogous reversals. Validation on other probing tasks is needed to confirm generality. We recommend that probing studies report results under at least two complementary layer selection criteria, and that five-metric ablations (or at minimum, results at multiple candidate layers spanning shallow, middle, and deep positions) become standard practice. Even among unbiased metrics, the choice between threshold-based and threshold-free criteria affects layer selection: AUROC peaks at mid-depth layers (${\sim}50\%$) while precision peaks at deep layers ($>90\%$), further demonstrating that layer selection methodology is a critical researcher degree of freedom. The cost of ablation is modest: evaluating five metrics across all layers adds minutes to an experiment that takes hours. The alternative is that conclusions about representational structure reflect layer selection methodology rather than the phenomenon under study. The control task provides independent corroboration: R1-32B selectivity increases from 7.5pp at the biased layer (L10) to 19.7pp at the corrected layer (L63), confirming that the biased metric selected layers where positional features dominate over genuine safety structure.
sections/discussion.tex:7:Information-theoretic reasoning suggests that hidden states (4096 to 5120 dimensions of internal computation) should dominate text features (384-dimensional sentence embeddings) purely by signal capacity. Both temporal context and modality choice significantly improve detection, but their relative magnitudes differ by scale. On R1-8B, the modality advantage (precision +22.4pp at $W{=}1$) exceeds the temporal improvement (+12.9pp from $W{=}1$ to $W{=}25$), establishing that modality choice matters more than temporal context at this scale. At 32B, the relative magnitudes depend on model and window size (\cref{sec:temporal}). Text probes benefit more from temporal context than HS probes because they start from a weaker single-step baseline and extract proportionally more from observing multi-step progressions. Safety commitment is a gradual process: the model progressively consolidates its intent over multiple reasoning steps rather than switching abruptly at a single token. Both modalities benefit from temporal context; for text probes, the improvement is universal across all four models. The practical implication is that temporal windowing ($W{=}3$ to $15$) remains the most robust single default for safety monitoring, as it provides guaranteed improvement regardless of modality, while the modality choice requires principled layer selection to realize its full potential.
sections/discussion.tex:13:Based on these findings, we recommend temporal windowing ($W{=}3$ to $15$) combined with principled layer selection (pure balanced accuracy or precision as the selection metric, never crossing rate) as defaults for deployment. At 7-8B, HS probes Pareto-dominate text probes: +22.4pp precision on R1-8B and +21.9pp on OT-7B, with lower FPR and comparable timing. At 32B, HS probes are statistically superior across all metrics, but practical trade-offs require model-specific decisions between lead time, coverage, and significance breadth. All current methods produce high FPR on safe traces at standard operating thresholds (39--52\% across methods on R1-8B), which means they characterize the safety commitment phenomenon rather than constitute production-ready detectors. The 85.5\% oracle gap (the fraction of theoretical early detection potential not captured by the best learned method) indicates that passive monitoring captures only a small portion of available signal (\cref{sec:oracle}). The gap between learned probes (+4.5 steps lead) and the oracle (+31 steps lead) suggests that hidden states at step $t$ encode the model's current safety state but carry limited predictive power about future trajectory evolution. Future work should explore active intervention through activation patching at candidate commitment points, expansion to multilingual and multi-turn settings, and evaluation at intermediate scales (13B, 70B) to determine whether the R1-32B dimensionality constraint reflects small-sample limitations or a fundamental property of distilled reasoning models.
sections/experiments.tex:11:\cref{tab:layer_selection} shows that the biased composite metric (balanced accuracy $\times$ crossing rate) systematically selects shallow layers for 32B models: L2 (3\% depth) for QwQ-32B and L10 (16\%) for R1-32B. Four unbiased metrics (pure balanced accuracy, precision, inverse FPR, additive composite) converge on deep layers: L60 (94\%) and L63 (98\%). Metrics from two measurement families (accuracy-based and false-positive-based) agree. The mechanism is that shallow layers produce more volatile representations, inflating crossing rate independently of discriminative power (\cref{sec:layer-sensitivity}).
sections/experiments.tex:52:HS probes significantly outperform text probes on all four models across all three metrics (\cref{tab:hs_vs_text}). Precision gains range from +15.4pp (R1-32B) to +23.6pp (QwQ-32B). The advantage is consistent across architectures (Llama vs.\ Qwen) and training methods (R1 distillation vs.\ STILL). Control task selectivity confirms genuine safety signal: 12.5--19.7pp above chance across all models (\cref{app:control}).
sections/experiments.tex:56:\paragraph{Caveats.} R1-32B achieves significance only at $W{=}1$ with 25\% coverage (5/20 traces); at $W{\geq}3$, dimensionality ($51200 \times W$ for $n{=}20$) prevents significance. QwQ-32B HS lead time is negative ($-$1.2 to +1.9 steps vs.\ text 3.7--12.3 steps): higher precision at later detection. On benign traces, probes produce 39--52\% false alarm rates, indicating that current methods characterize the commitment phenomenon rather than constitute production-ready detectors. Per-model details in \cref{sec:32b-analysis}.
sections/experiments.tex:60:Temporal windowing ($W{>}1$) improves both modalities on all four models (\cref{fig:window_ablation}).
